title: Isandro and the Prom
premise: Coral Dunmore has survived high school by being forgettable, but when his late grandmother's recipe box yields coded instructions instead of pie crusts, he learns she was part of a student group that exposed the school board's cover-up of a toxic contamination in the 1970s—and that they were silenced, one by one. Following her clues through the school's sealed archives, Coral recruits the misfits he's spent years avoiding, including prom committee outsider Junie Vale, whose mother was the last whistleblower. As prom night approaches, Coral must choose between staying invisible and reading his grandmother's suppressed findings aloud where no one can look away. The book ends with Coral winning the argument he could never win at home—not by debating, but by refusing to stop speaking—while the board resigns and Coral finally feels he belongs, not because he was seen, but because he chose to be seen.
about_author: Edmund Eastwick is a former high school debate coach who spent a decade watching quiet students carry loud secrets. He writes in a converted garage in coastal Oregon, where he keeps his own grandmother's recipe box on the windowsill.

chapters.title: Head Down, Grades Up
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. We meet Coral mid-debate tournament, winning effortlessly, then watch him go silent at the dinner table where his father's temper rules. Establishes his invisibility strategy and the ache of winning everywhere except home. Emotional beat: competent outside, cowed inside.

chapters.title: The Recipe Box
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, sorting his late grandmother's kitchen for the estate sale. He finds a recipe card for 'Board Stew' whose ingredients are names, dates, and a locker number. The card is dated three days before her death. Emotional beat: curiosity cracking open grief.

chapters.title: Locker 114
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The locker belongs to dead student Marcus Ives, class of 1979. Inside: a mimeographed newsletter, 'The Ledger,' alleging the board buried water contamination tests. A janitor catches him and goes pale at the name Ives. Emotional beat: first vertigo of the buried past.

chapters.title: The Argument at Home
chapters.summary: Coral tries to mention the find at dinner; his father shuts it down with the family rule—never make waves. Coral's mother quietly slides him a napkin with a phone number written in his grandmother's handwriting. Emotional beat: loyalty to family vs. pull of truth.

chapters.title: Junie Vale, Prom Committee
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. The one student louder than Coral is quiet: Junie, banned from prom planning for asking too many budget questions. Coral recognizes a fellow keeper of grievances. She reveals her mother, Delia, was on the Ledger staff. Emotional beat: two loners circling an alliance.

chapters.title: Delia's Silence
chapters.summary: Coral and Junie visit Delia, now a night-shift nurse, who refuses to talk—until she sees the 'Board Stew' card and goes white. She gives them one sentence: 'Your grandmother was the one who never stopped writing.' Emotional beat: the cost of survival made visible.

chapters.title: The Sealed Archive
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Using the janitor's guilt and a borrowed key, they reach the school's dead-files room and find the 1979 water test results—numbers that don't match the published ones. Someone has already been through the box; a page is missing. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by surveillance.

chapters.title: Recruiting the Misfits
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, rotating close-third. The group grows: Theo the archivist nerd, Priya the journalist who's been suspended once already, Marcus Ives's nephew Ray. Coral, the boy who avoids teams, finds himself building one. Emotional beat: the terrifying warmth of belonging.

chapters.title: What the Water Did
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Research montage: illness clusters, a shuttered clinic, teachers who transferred out mid-year. The contamination never fully stopped—the old pipes are still in the east wing. Emotional beat: this isn't history, it's ongoing.

chapters.title: The Board Notices
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral is called in—first gently, then not—by Vice Principal Harrow, a 1979 graduate who was on the Ledger too before flipping sides. Threats arrive dressed as college recommendation offers. Emotional beat: the price of survival, itemized.

chapters.title: Father and Son
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. His father discovers the copied documents and explodes: 'You think they didn't ruin us once already?' Coral learns the family's silence has a history—his grandfather was the plant worker who first reported the contamination. Emotional beat: inherited fear named at last.

chapters.title: The Missing Page
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Delia finally breaks: the missing page names which board members took payments, and it's been in her possession for forty years, hidden inside a prom photo album. She's been waiting for someone brave enough to ask. Emotional beat: guilt handed to a new generation.

chapters.title: Prom as Battlefield
chapters.summary: Group POV, quick cuts. The board announces the east wing will be 'renovated' over summer—demolishing the evidence and the pipes. The team realizes the only public gathering left before demolition is prom. Emotional beat: the clock starts audibly ticking.

chapters.title: Infiltration, With Corsages
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The plan: get on the prom committee, get the microphone, get the page photocopied and distributed in the programs. Coral, master of invisibility, must now perform visibility. Junie teaches him to waltz; the scene crackles. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Dead Files
chapters.summary: Ray's POV. Someone tips off Harrow; the archive is emptied overnight and Theo is suspended for 'trespassing.' Ray discovers the leak came from inside—Priya traded information to save her college acceptance. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth turns inward, painfully.

chapters.title: The Fracture
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The group splinters; Junie wants to go public now, half-cocked. Coral, who spent the whole book avoiding conflict, must hold the team together by admitting his own fear—his father's voice in his mouth. Emotional beat: leadership through vulnerability.

chapters.title: Harrow's Confession
chapters.summary: Harrow's POV, the book's one departure. A flashback to 1979: young Harrow watching his friends get destroyed, choosing safety, spending forty years as a lock on a door. He returns the missing page to Coral, saying only, 'She never stopped writing either.' Emotional beat: the price of survival, paid in full.

chapters.title: Prom Night
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Gowns, punch, chaperones—and a photocopied page in every program. The board arrives to give a toast. Coral takes the microphone meant for announcements. Emotional beat: held breath, the whole book converging on one moment.

chapters.title: The Speech
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. He reads his grandmother's findings aloud—not as debate, but as testimony—while students stand, then parents, then teachers, then Delia in her nurse's scrubs. Harrow corroborates on the record. Emotional beat: the quiet kid wins the argument by refusing to stop speaking.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Board resignations, an independent water audit, the east wing tested instead of demolished. Priya faces consequences but owns them; Theo's suspension is reversed. Coral's father, in the crowd, doesn't applaud—but he doesn't look away either. Emotional beat: victory that costs, and is worth it.

chapters.title: The Recipe Box, Reopened
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. At home, Coral and his mother cook from his grandmother's actual recipes—the real ones, the pie crusts and stews—for the first time since her death. His father sits down at the table and stays. Emotional beat: grief and belonging reconciled over dinner.

chapters.title: Coral Dunmore, Visible
chapters.summary: Coral's final POV. At the re-formed Ledger's first meeting, Coral is asked to write the editorial. He signs his full name. The last image: the recipe box on his windowsill, one new card inside—'Board Stew, serves everyone.' Emotional beat: invisibility chosen, then unchosen, forever.
